title: Co-designing AI Education Curriculum with Cross-Disciplinary High School Teachers
venue: AAAI-24 (The Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school teachers from different disciplines think about teaching about and with artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative AI, in their classrooms. The authors are motivated by the rapid rise of public-facing AI tools such as ChatGPT and DALL·E and by the challenge of creating AI curriculum that works across subject areas rather than only in computer science. The central question is how teachers interpret AI in relation to disciplinary goals and what opportunities and challenges they see in using AI tools for instruction.

The study used a co-design approach: five collaborative sessions were conducted with eight high school teachers teaching humanities and STEM subjects, including social studies, English/ELA, economics, art, engineering, statistics, and computer science. The sessions were held over Zoom across four months, and the teachers reviewed and adapted AI curriculum resources on topics such as AI in everyday life, facial recognition, generative AI in art, AI and math/data, and AI and society. The sessions were designed to let teachers critique resources and develop their own lesson ideas, with generative AI becoming a stronger focus in later sessions after ChatGPT and DALL·E gained prominence.

The teachers generally framed AI through both technical and ethical lenses, but the relative emphasis varied by discipline. For example, engineering and CS-oriented teachers emphasized technical structure and model behavior, while English and social studies teachers were more interested in ethical argumentation, social impact, and disciplinary frameworks such as SOAPSTone or OPCVL. Several teachers saw value in a "dual exploration" approach, where students use their subject-specific analytic frameworks to examine AI-generated content and simultaneously learn about the limitations and assumptions of AI. Overall, the paper concludes that AI curriculum can be made more adaptable and meaningful when it is co-designed with teachers across disciplines and aligned with both technical and ethical goals.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools built on large language models and image-generation models, used to generate or transform text and images.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers co-designed AI curriculum and discussed using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and DALL·E in high school lessons across art, math, social studies, English, engineering, and economics; the paper focused on teachers' perspectives on teaching with and about generative AI rather than evaluating student outcomes.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, formative co-design study with eight high school teachers. It provides rich descriptive evidence but no experimental comparison or causal effect estimate.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable outcome effects on students or teachers. Its contribution is conceptual and design-oriented, so impact is meaningful but not quantified.
